title_en: Teenagers Win National Prize with Solar Boat
title_ru: Подростки выиграли национальную премию с лодкой на солнечной энергии
description_ru: Вымышленная новость: школьники из Таллоуфилда построили лодку на солнечных батареях, которая убирает водоросли с озера.
text:
A group of teenagers from a small school in northern Eastmere has won the national Young Engineers Award with a boat that runs entirely on sunlight. The students, who attend Tallowfield High School, beat more than three hundred teams from across the country with their design, which they have named the Sunskipper. The judges described the project as "practical, clever and wonderfully well built", and the winners will now represent the country at an international competition next spring.

The idea began last year in a physics lesson, when teacher Hannah Crowley asked her class to think of a problem in their own town. The students quickly agreed on one: the lake in the town park, which is popular with families, is covered with weeds every summer, and the council cannot afford to pay for machines to clear them. "We wanted to find a cheap and clean way to do it," said sixteen-year-old Tomas Reeve, the leader of the team. "Most weed cutters use petrol, which pollutes the water, so we decided to use the sun."

Over the following eight months, the six students worked every Thursday after school and during most of their holidays. They started with a flat plastic boat that had been thrown away by a local sailing club, and they covered it with solar panels bought with money from a bake sale. Then they added a small electric motor and a set of rotating blades at the front. When the boat moves slowly across the surface, the blades cut the weeds and push them into a net, which can be emptied on the shore. "Our first test was a disaster," said fifteen-year-old Priya Nandakumar, who designed the electronics. "The boat spun in circles for twenty minutes, and then it sank."

After that failure, the team decided to ask for help. They wrote to a retired engineer called Walter Bright, who used to build ships, and he agreed to meet them every week. "At first they argued so much that I thought I would go home," he said with a laugh. "But they listened to advice, and that is the most important skill for any engineer." With his help, they changed the shape of the hull, moved the motor, and added a simple sensor that stops the blades if something gets caught. If they had not made these changes, the boat would never have completed its trials.

The Sunskipper has now cleaned about a third of the lake. In a recent test, it removed two hundred kilograms of weeds in a single afternoon, and it needed no fuel at all. The council has already asked the students whether a second boat could be built for another lake on the edge of town. Councillor Marcus Bell said that the project had saved the town about twelve thousand pounds so far. "We have been trying to solve this problem for years," he said. "It took a group of teenagers to find the answer."

The national competition took place last weekend in the city of Harbourgate. Each team had ten minutes to present its work to a panel of professional engineers, and then to demonstrate it in a large water tank. Many entries were very impressive, including an automatic greenhouse and a bicycle that charges mobile phones. Even so, the judges said that the Sunskipper stood out because it solved a real local problem and could easily be copied by other towns. "It is not a fantasy machine," said head judge Dr Eleanor Marsh. "It is something that a community can use tomorrow."

The students are not planning to rest. They are currently raising money for their trip abroad, and the headteacher, Ian Prescott, has said that the school will pay for the tickets if the team cannot collect enough. In the meantime, they hope to improve the boat by adding a camera, which would allow the operator to steer it from the shore. Priya Nandakumar also wants to teach younger pupils how to build a simple version. "If we can inspire a few younger students, then we have really won," she said.

Local people have also joined in. On Sunday afternoon, dozens of families gathered at the lake to watch the Sunskipper at work. Children waved from the bank, and a few brave dog owners threw sticks to see whether the boat would avoid them. It did. As the sun sank behind the trees, Tomas Reeve picked up the trophy, which is shaped like a small golden gear, and held it above his head. "We are only a small school," he said, "but we have shown that good ideas can come from anywhere."
